title: Fighting the Cancer of a Recklessly Negative Attitude
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article warns leaders about how quickly negativity spreads when a low-performing, poor-attitude team member finds allies among other dissatisfied colleagues, forming what the author calls a 'cabal of complaints.' The piece distinguishes tolerable underperformance (low skill with a good attitude, worth coaching) from the combination the author warns leaders not to slow-walk: low skill paired with a negative, blame-externalizing attitude. The central argument is that patience here is a mistake — leaders who try to coach the attitude away rather than acting decisively allow the negativity to metastasize through the team. The closing line frames a second negative performer as evidence the leader acted too slowly.
points: Low performers with negative attitudes tend to find and reinforce each other quickly, forming a growing 'cabal of complaints' that pulls in newer or borderline team members.
Leaders who try to coach up a low performer's poor attitude too patiently allow the negativity to spread before they finally act.
Terminating a negative low performer can look punitive to the group they've cultivated, but slow-walking the decision does more long-term damage.
The author distinguishes tolerable low skill (worth coaching) from the combination of low skill and negative attitude (not worth tolerating).
quotes: It’s simply astonishing how quickly the lowest performers find each other. They seek each other out for validation, effectively forming a cabal of complaints and grievances.
By infecting others with their conspiracy theories and complaints, they build a wall of support around themselves, which is hard for leaders to break through.
A low-performing team member with a negative attitude is a cancer that can spread quickly and destroy the positivity of a team or culture.
If an attitude is a decision, then those who mindfully make a bad one seldom revoke it. Especially when they are failing.
If there are now two low performers with a negative attitude, the leader didn’t act fast enough.
